instructions:
Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US high school student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 395 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool compared the draft with essays that students wrote on other assignments. Use its report when you revise:

Tone check against human essay writing (398 words). Distance from the human centre: 1.39 (1.0 is typical for a human text).
- negative charge: 26.9 (dolors per 1,000 words); most human texts are between 2.69 and 20.55. The draft uses more negative words than people do here.
- net charge: 31.47 (per 1,000 words); most human texts are between 49.88 and 107.19. The overall tone is more negative than human writing of this kind.
- positive charge: 58.37 (hedons per 1,000 words); most human texts are between 63.19 and 114.1. The draft uses fewer positive words than people do here.
Inside the human range: total charge, positive plus negative; words that carry charge; charge under a negation; charge after an intensifier such as 'very'; charge after a contrast word such as 'but'; net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean; how unevenly charge is spread over sentences.
These are ranges, not targets. Change wording only where the change also makes the text more specific or more honest.

Draft:

Drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, with the narrow exception of a phone that is mounted and used for navigation before the trip begins. The reasoning is simple: driving demands a person's full attention, and a phone is built to take it away.

Most people believe they can handle a quick glance at a screen. The numbers say otherwise. Looking away from the road for just five seconds at highway speed means traveling the length of a football field without watching what is ahead. A text message, a song change, or a notification can easily cost that much time. Crashes caused by distraction injure and kill thousands of people each year, and many of the victims are passengers, pedestrians, and other drivers who never made the choice to take the risk.

Some argue that hands-free calling solves the problem. It does not. Research on attention shows that the danger comes largely from the mind, not the hands. A driver in an intense conversation can look straight at a stoplight and still fail to register that it has turned red. Talking to someone who is not in the car, and cannot see the traffic, pulls thought away from the task of driving. Voice-controlled texting and hands-free calls feel safer, but the delay in reaction time is similar to that of handheld use.

Others say a total ban is too strict, since phones now hold maps, music, and emergency tools. That concern is fair, and it is why a limited allowance makes sense. A driver can enter a destination before leaving, mount the device, and follow spoken directions. A driver facing a real emergency can pull over safely and call for help. These uses do not require attention to be pulled from the road while the car is moving.

Laws also matter because personal discipline often fails. Many drivers admit that distracting behavior is dangerous and then do it anyway. Clear rules with real penalties change habits, much as seat belt laws did decades ago. Few people today would argue that buckling up is an unreasonable burden.

A phone call or a message can almost always wait ten minutes. A life cannot be given back. For that reason, drivers should keep their phones out of their hands and out of their minds until the vehicle is parked.
